The sending device reads a local file and flashes it out as an animated\nsequence of optical codes. The\narchitecture keeps that layer swappable.\n\n## Why\n\nThe screen-to-camera channel is the one data path that survives when everything\nelse is unavailable or untrusted:\n\n- **Air-gapped systems** — the receiving machine is deliberately not on any network.\n- **Hostile or captive networks** — hotel wifi, conference NAT, corporate DLP.\n- **Cross-ecosystem transfer** — AirDrop doesn't talk to Android; Nearby Share doesn't talk to iOS.\n- **No pairing, no accounts, no cloud** — nothing is uploaded anywhere, because\n  there is nowhere to upload it to. The bytes go from screen to lens.\n- **Provably no exfiltration** — a static page with no network calls can be\n  audited once and trusted thereafter.\n\n## The hard part\n\nThe channel is **strictly one-way**. The sender has no idea how the receiver is\ndoing — there is no ACK, no retransmit request, no back-channel of any kind. The\nreceiver *will* miss frames: autofocus hunting, motion blur, glare, the user\nlooking away.\n\nA naive \"loop through chunks 1..N forever\" transfer degrades badly under loss\n(the coupon-collector problem — the last few chunks take agonizingly long).\nscreenferry's design centers on **rateless erasure coding**: the sender emits an\nendless stream of encoded frames, and the receiver reconstructs the file once it\nhas collected *any* sufficient subset. Miss a frame and it simply doesn't\nmatter — the next one is just as useful.\n\n## Status\n\n**Research complete. Phase 1 core codec built (22 tests green). In Chromium the practical limits are the blob-storage quotas\nabove: over the in-memory limit, blobs page to disk rather than failing, so a multi-hundred-MB\nblob URL works on desktop but will thrash on a 2 GB Android phone (20 MB in-memory limit). The\noften-cited \"500 MB blob cap\" is historical Chromium behaviour from ~2014–2015 and no longer\napplies. Safari does not document a limit; assume the constraint is device RAM, since iOS is\naggressive about killing memory-hungry web content.\n\nSince screenferry's realistic maximum payload is single-digit megabytes (§6), blob URL size is a\nnon-issue in practice. Document it and move on.\n\n### 2.4 Should we stream to disk for large files?\n\n**Yes on desktop Chromium, and use OPFS as the universal staging buffer everywhere else.**\n","numLines":100,"startLine":300,"totalLines":2362}}}

That is the one cross-platform\n636\twrite-then-hand-off pipeline that exists.\n637\t\n638\t### 3.7 Single self-contained HTML file as an alternative distribution\n639\t\n640\tExtremely attractive for this app: one `screenferry.html` the user saves to a USB stick or their\n641\tDownloads folder and can open forever, with no server, no service worker, no cache eviction, no\n642\tinstall flow. It is the true air-gap artefact.\n643\t\n644\t**What works:**\n645\t\n646\t- Inlining JS and CSS into one HTML file is a solved problem —\n647\t  [`vite-plugin-singlefile`](https://github.com/richardtallent/vite-plugin-singlefile) does\n648\t  exactly this and explicitly names this use case: *\"this can be very handy for offline web\n649\t  applications — apps bundled into a single HTML file that you can double-click and open directly\n650\t  in your web browser, no server needed.\"*\n651\t- `file://` **is a secure context.** MDN: *\"a secure context is a page loaded using HTTPS or the\n652\t  `file:///` URL scheme, or a page loaded from localhost\"*\n653\t  ([MDN: getUserMedia](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevices/getUserMedia),\n654\t  [MDN: Secure Contexts](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Defenses/Secure_Contexts)).\n655\t  A May 2025 W3C WebRTC thread questioning `getDisplayMedia()` from `file://` frames the spec as\n656\t  *currently permitting* it\n657\t  ([public-webrtc archive](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-webrtc/2025May/0002.html)) —\n658\t  corroboration that the path is real, and a { \"isSecureContext\": true, \"origin\": \"file://\",\n665\t    \"hasMediaDevices\": true, \"hasGUM\": true,\n666\t    \"hasShowOpenFilePicker\": true, \"hasShowSaveFilePicker\": true,\n667\t    \"hasStorageGetDirectory\": true, \"hasWakeLock\": true,\n668\t    \"hasRVFC\": true, \"hasBarcodeDetector\": false }\n669\t  ```\n670\t\n671\t  So on Chromium the camera path, the file pickers, OPFS, `navigator.serviceWorker.register('./sw.js')` rejects with\n679\t  `TypeError: Failed to register a ServiceWorker: The URL protocol of the current origin ('null')\n680\t  is not supported.` Not a real denied means the UA\nmay clear it under storage pressure. *\"The browser may or may not honor the request, depending on\nbrowser-specific rules\"* — Chromium grants it silently based on engagement/installed-PWA\nheuristics; Firefox prompts. It requires a secure context and is **not available in Web Workers**.\n\nTwo important limits for screenferry:\n\n- Persisted storage protects against **eviction under storage pressure**. It does **not**\n  demonstrably override WebKit's 7-day ITP deletion (§3.2), which is a privacy mechanism, not a\n  quota mechanism. Do not treat `persist()` as a substitute for Add-to-Home-Screen on iOS.\n- It also protects the OPFS staging file used for partial receives (§2.4), which is the more\n  practical benefit.\n\n**OPFS support is the good news of this whole document:** MDN marks the Origin Private File\nSystem **\"Baseline Widely available\"** — available across browsers since **March 2023**\n([MDN OPFS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/File_System_API/Origin_private_file_system)),\nwith WebKit shipping it in Safari 15.2 / iOS 15.2. `createWritable()` works on the main thread;\n`createSyncAccessHandle()` (much faster, synchronous) works **only in a worker**. And crucially\n`fileHandle.getFile()` returns a real `File`, which drops straight into\n`navigator.share({files:[file]})` or an `<a download>`. That is the one cross-platform\nwrite-then-hand-off pipeline that exists.\n\n### 3.7 Single self-contained HTML file as an alternative distribution\n\nExtremely attractive for this app: one `screenferry.html` the user saves to a USB stick or their\nDownloads folder and can open forever, with no server, no service worker, no cache eviction, no\ninstall flow. It is the true air-gap artefact.\n\n**What works:**\n\n- Inlining JS and CSS into one HTML file is a solved problem —\n Secure Contexts](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Defenses/Secure_Contexts)).\n  A May 2025 W3C WebRTC thread questioning `getDisplayMedia()` from `file://` frames the spec as\n  *currently permitting* it\n  ([public-webrtc archive](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-webrtc/2025May/0002.html)) —\n  corroboration that the path is real, and a warning that it is under scrutiny.\n\n  **Verified empirically** (Chrome for Testing 151.0.7922.34, Linux, page loaded from a\n  `file:///…/probe.html`):\n\n  ```json\n  { \"isSecureContext\": true, \"origin\": \"file://\",\n
